title: The Art of Simplicity in Software Design
content:
As developers, we often fall into the trap of over-engineering solutions. We reach for complex architectures, add layers of abstraction, and introduce dependencies before we need them. But some of the best software ever built is remarkably simple.

Complexity is the Enemy

Every line of code you write is a line of code you have to maintain. Every dependency you add is a potential point of failure. Every abstraction layer is another thing a new team member has to understand.

This doesn't mean we should write naive code. It means we should be intentional about the complexity we introduce.

Rules I Try to Follow

  1. Start simple — Build the simplest thing that works. You can always add complexity later.
  2. YAGNI — You Aren't Gonna Need It. Don't build features or abstractions you don't need right now.
  3. Measure first — Don't optimize without data. Profile before you refactor.
  4. Delete code — The best code is the code that doesn't exist. Regularly prune dead code.

A Practical Example

This very blog stores its posts as JSON files on disk. No database, no ORM, no migration scripts. Could it use a database? Sure. Does it need one? Not yet. When the time comes, the data layer is abstracted enough that swapping in a database would be straightforward.

That's the sweet spot: simple enough for now, flexible enough for later.
